units.title: Unit 17 — Student life
learningObjectives: Use precise collocations to describe admissions, university courses and academic qualifications.
Distinguish expressions for academic achievement from phrases for attention, motivation and attendance.
Identify register restrictions in expressions such as read a subject and play truant.
Produce natural combinations for scholarships, grades, study habits and classroom evaluations.

items.example: The scholarship panel was impressed by the candidate's mental agility.
items.note: Mental agility is the ability to think clearly and respond quickly.

items.example: The city offers additional science workshops for gifted children.
items.note: Gifted describes exceptional intellectual or creative ability rather than good behaviour.

items.example: She hopes to win a scholarship for her postgraduate studies.
items.note: Win a scholarship means receive educational funding through merit or selection.

items.pt: aluno que só tira notas máximas
items.example: Despite her demanding timetable, Maya remains a straight-A student.
items.note: Straight-A refers to consistently achieving top grades in a letter-grade system.

items.example: Students can apply to a university before their final results arrive.
items.note: Apply to names the institution receiving an application; apply for names the place or course sought.

items.example: A strong portfolio may help you secure a place on the programme.
items.note: Secure a place means successfully obtain admission, often amid competition.

items.pt: cursar uma disciplina ou área acadêmica
items.example: In traditional British usage, you can read a subject at university.
items.note: Read meaning study a subject is formal, chiefly British, and now somewhat old-fashioned.

items.example: The new academic year begins with an orientation programme.
items.note: Academic year refers to the teaching period, not necessarily the calendar year.

items.example: All engineering students must take the same core subjects.
items.note: Core subjects are required elements shared by students on a course.

items.example: The lecturer published the list of set texts before the semester.
items.note: Set texts are books or passages officially prescribed for study.

items.example: Several distinguished scholars reviewed the new research proposal.
items.note: Distinguished signals recognised academic achievement and reputation.

items.example: The conference attracted leading authorities in climate modelling.
items.note: A leading authority is widely respected for expertise in a particular field.

items.example: Many students plan to graduate from university next summer.
items.note: Use graduate from to identify the university where a degree was completed.

items.example: Online courses helped her return to formal education after years at work.
items.note: Formal education refers to organised schooling or accredited academic study.

items.example: You can sign up for a course through the learning portal.
items.note: Sign up for is relatively informal; enrol on a course is also common in British English.

items.example: Employees may enrol on a course in technical writing.
items.note: Enrol on is common in British English; American usage often prefers enroll in.

items.example: The college runs evening courses for people who work during the day.
items.note: Evening courses are scheduled after typical working hours.

items.example: Applicants must meet the entry requirements before they can register.
items.note: Meet requirements is the standard combination for satisfying stated conditions.

items.pt: estudantes adultos que ingressam mais tarde
items.example: The university provides flexible timetables for mature students.
items.note: In British education, mature students enter higher education later than usual.

items.example: He intends to complete a degree while working part-time.
items.note: Complete a degree means finish the required academic programme successfully.

items.example: Her writing has shown marked improvement since the first assessment.
items.note: Marked signals a clear and noticeable improvement, not merely a small change.

items.example: His attention wanders when the instructions become repetitive.
items.note: Attention wanders describes a temporary loss of focus.

items.example: The teacher noticed his natural talent for solving spatial puzzles.
items.note: Natural talent suggests an ability that appears without extensive prior training.

items.example: With careful checking, it is possible to achieve full marks on the quiz.
items.note: Full marks means the maximum possible score, particularly in British English.

items.example: The presentation was clear, but there is room for improvement in the visuals.
items.note: This tactful expression signals weaknesses without dismissing the whole result.

items.example: Students who learn by heart may recall definitions without understanding them.
items.note: Learn by heart means memorise exactly, not just understand the material.

items.example: Her thirst for knowledge led her to explore subjects beyond the syllabus.
items.note: Thirst for knowledge conveys strong intellectual curiosity.

items.example: The new trainee is a quick learner who needs little guidance.
items.note: Quick learner is a conventional way to praise someone who learns rapidly.

items.example: His concentration wavers after an hour of uninterrupted lectures.
items.note: Waver describes attention becoming unsteady rather than disappearing completely.

items.example: Candidates must demonstrate an ability to interpret numerical data.
items.note: Demonstrate an ability is formal assessment language for showing a skill.

items.example: Junior researchers who show initiative can take responsibility for new tasks.
items.note: Show initiative means act constructively without being told exactly what to do.

items.example: The candidate has proven ability in managing international projects.
items.note: Proven ability indicates competence supported by past results or experience.

items.pt: matar aula; faltar à escola sem autorização
items.example: The headteacher warned that pupils who play truant may face sanctions.
items.note: Play truant is chiefly British for being absent from school without permission.

items.example: Children in the district are required to attend school regularly.
items.note: Attend school refers to being present as a pupil; it is not the same as attend to a task.

items.example: Students acquire knowledge through practice, reading and discussion.
items.note: Acquire knowledge is a natural formal combination; get knowledge is less idiomatic here.

items.example: Consistent feedback helps beginners make progress in pronunciation.
items.note: Make progress is the idiomatic verb-noun combination; do progress is not.

items.example: Applicants may get a place on a competitive course after an interview.
items.note: Get a place is a more conversational alternative to secure a place.

items.example: Historic seats of learning often maintain libraries of rare books.
items.note: Seat of learning is a formal or literary expression for an educational institution.

units.title: Unit 18 — Writing essays, assignments and reports
learningObjectives: Describe the stages of a research project using conventional academic collocations.
Express a research claim cautiously and support conclusions with appropriately described evidence.
Distinguish a working hypothesis, literature review, critique and critical analysis.
Use natural formal expressions to formulate, test and defend arguments in reports.

items.example: You must submit a report to the supervisor by Friday afternoon.
items.note: Submit is the standard formal verb for handing in assessed academic work.

items.example: Researchers will present findings at the departmental seminar.
items.note: Present findings is a natural academic expression for communicating study results.

items.example: First, select a research topic that can be investigated with available data.
items.note: Select a research topic describes the initial decision that defines the study's focus.

items.example: Before collecting data, the team will formulate a working hypothesis.
items.note: Formulate is a formal verb for expressing a preliminary, testable proposition.

items.example: A working hypothesis helps the team decide which observations matter.
items.note: A working hypothesis is provisional and may be revised as evidence develops.

items.example: The latest measurements appear to support a hypothesis about heat loss.
items.note: Evidence may support a hypothesis; avoid claiming it has proved one absolutely.

items.example: The laboratory agreed to undertake a study of the new materials.
items.note: Undertake a study is relatively formal; do a study is more conversational.

items.example: The protocol was revised to comply with research ethics guidelines.
items.note: Research ethics concerns accepted standards for conducting research responsibly.

items.example: A literature review should compare earlier work rather than merely list papers.
items.note: A literature review synthesises existing scholarship relevant to a research question.

items.example: Some background reading will help you narrow the scope of the project.
items.note: Background reading builds initial understanding before detailed research or writing.

items.example: The article offers an in-depth critique of the methodology used.
items.note: In-depth signals a detailed, analytical examination rather than a brief summary.

items.example: The introduction should reflect current research on the topic.
items.note: Current research refers to scholarship relevant at the present stage of a field.

items.example: The proposal must provide a rationale for choosing this sample.
items.note: A rationale explains the reasons for a decision, approach or study.

items.example: Authors should back up conclusions with evidence from reliable experiments.
items.note: Back up is a phrasal verb meaning substantiate a claim with support.

items.example: Writers should not exaggerate a claim beyond what their results justify.
items.note: An exaggerated claim presents stronger certainty or significance than the evidence permits.

items.example: Please lay out results in a table before discussing the trends.
items.note: Lay out means arrange information clearly, often in tables or diagrams.

items.example: The author tries to make the case for additional public investment.
items.note: Make the case for means present reasons supporting a proposal or position.

items.example: The essay offers a vigorous defence of community-led research.
items.note: Vigorous strengthens defence by suggesting a forceful, energetic argument.

items.example: The report must confront an issue that earlier studies ignored.
items.note: Confront an issue means face a difficult question directly instead of avoiding it.

items.pt: enfrentar e tratar de uma questão
items.example: A useful literature review should tackle an issue left unresolved by previous work.
items.note: Tackle highlights practical engagement with a difficult problem.

items.example: This short article cannot provide an exhaustive account of the entire debate.
items.note: Exhaustive means comprehensive; it does not mean tiring or exhausted.

items.example: Recent research indicates that the intervention may be effective.
items.note: Research indicates introduces findings cautiously without guaranteeing certainty.

items.example: A scientist may formulate a theory to explain repeated observations.
items.note: Formulate a theory means develop and express a coherent explanatory framework.

items.example: The team designed a second experiment to test a theory about sensor drift.
items.note: Test a theory means examine it against observations; it does not imply proving it.

items.pt: abordar muitos aspectos de um assunto
items.example: The review manages to cover a lot of ground without losing its focus.
items.note: Cover a lot of ground means discuss many topics or aspects in limited space.

items.pt: a ideia central de um argumento
items.example: The thrust of an argument can be lost among too many examples.
items.note: Thrust refers to the main point or direction of an argument, not physical force.

items.example: Interviewers sought witnesses with first-hand knowledge of the incident.
items.note: First-hand knowledge comes from direct experience rather than reports by others.

items.example: The assignment calls for critical analysis of the conflicting findings.
items.note: Critical analysis assesses strengths and weaknesses; it is not merely negative commentary.

items.example: Students often do research before drafting their dissertations.
items.note: Do research is the standard collocation; make research is generally non-idiomatic.

items.example: The committee requested a full explanation of the inconsistent results.
items.note: Full explanation indicates comprehensive reasons or details, not necessarily an exhaustive study.

items.example: The study has not yet produced convincing evidence of a causal link.
items.note: Convincing evidence is sufficiently persuasive to support a claim.

items.pt: os argumentos a favor da mudança
items.example: The introduction sets out the case for change in the training system.
items.note: The case for something is the set of reasons supporting that proposal.

items.example: You must submit an assignment through the online portal.
items.note: Submit an assignment is the standard formal wording for handing in coursework.

items.example: An initial hypothesis should be revised if new evidence challenges it.
items.note: Initial describes a hypothesis proposed at the start rather than a final conclusion.
